items.body_md:
Today, Omnis Pleasants' docket recorded Dkts. 196–210: an employment application (Dkt. 196), a certificate of no objection (Dkt. 199), five exhibits (Dkts. 201–205), a hearing agenda (Dkt. 208), and six pro hac vice motions and admissions (Dkts. 198, 206, 207, 209, 210, and 200). The employment application at Dkt. 196 is the only filing on this list that warrants examination before tomorrow's § 341 meeting and the September 3 final hearing complex.

Dkt. 196 is a retention application filed August 31. The full text has not been pulled, so the identity of the applicant and the scope of the engagement are not confirmed from primary source. What is clear from context is that Omnis Fuel Technologies and Quantum Pleasants have already placed a contested objection on the record against the HSF Kramer retention (Dkt. 188, filed August 28), and the U.S. Trustee filed its own objection to that same application (Dkt. 175). Any additional professional retention application filed at this stage — two business days before a fully contested final hearing — carries at minimum procedural-and-important weight: it adds another contested item to the September 3 docket or establishes a professional whose fees will run against estate cash. The certificate of no objection at Dkt. 199 relates to an unspecified underlying motion; without the full text, no substantive conclusion follows, though the timing suggests it may concern one of the uncontested first-day orders already on the September 3 agenda. The five exhibits at Dkts. 201–205, also without pulled text, most likely supplement one of the pending contested motions — the cash collateral objection (Dkt. 172), the dismissal motion (Dkt. 93), or the bidding procedures objection (Dkt. 169) — given the volume and proximity to the hearing. The hearing agenda at Dkt. 208 confirms the September 3 contested final hearing is formally calendared; the agenda itself is procedural but its substance will reflect whether any of the open disputes have been resolved consensually before the hearing date. The six pro hac vice entries (Dkts. 198, 200, 206, 207, 209, 210) are procedural and routine.

The posture entering the final two days has not changed from yesterday's baseline: the September 3, 1:00 p.m. ET hearing before Judge Owens carries simultaneous contested issues on cash collateral (Dkts. 17, 50, opposed by Omnis Fuel Technologies / Quantum at Dkt. 172 and by WVEDA at Dkt. 171), wages and utilities (opposed or under objection deadline), critical vendor payments, bidding procedures (opposed at Dkt. 169), and HSF Kramer's retention (opposed by Omnis Fuel Technologies / Quantum at Dkt. 188 and by the U.S. Trustee at Dkt. 175). A final cash collateral order that materially deviates from the interim terms, or that the court declines to enter at all, is the highest-consequence outcome for recovery: the interim order at Dkt. 50 caps prepetition tax and fee disbursements at $775,000.00, ties all cash use to the adequate protection budget, and requires the sale process to continue — all of which unravel if the final order fails. 
The § 341 Meeting of Creditors is scheduled for September 2, 2026 at 1:00 p.m. ET via Zoom
, the day before the hearing complex.

items.body_md:
On August 31, Brandt Silverkorn of Edelson PC / Oppenheim + Zebrak filed a Transcript Designation Form (Dkt. 686) in the district court — the standard mechanism by which an appellant identifies, for the Ninth Circuit's record, which trial or hearing transcripts are to be prepared and transmitted as part of the appellate record. The filing is procedural, but in context it is worth flagging: it is the first concrete record-assembly step taken in either of the two pending fee appeals since the USCA Case Number entries (Dkts. 684–685) confirmed the Ninth Circuit had opened separate dockets for No. 26-5391 (Edelson PC / Oppenheim + Zebrak) and No. 26-5455 (Cowan DeBaets Abrahams & Sheppard LLP). 
No. 26-5391, filed August 18, appeals from the July 20 judgment (Dkt. 680) including all prior orders, with Edelson PC and Oppenheim + Zebrak intending to focus on the fee and expenses award.
 
No. 26-5455, filed August 19, also appeals from the July 20 judgment but is expressly limited to the district court's order granting in part the motion for attorneys' fees.
 The Transcript Designation Form was filed by Silverkorn — Edelson / O+Z counsel — which means Dkt. 686 is attributable to No. 26-5391; nothing on the district docket as of August 31 reflects a corresponding transcript designation from Cowan DeBaets.

The significance is limited but real. A transcript designation is procedural under FRAP 10(b) and Ninth Circuit Rule 10-3; it does not affect any party's legal rights or the class's recovery posture directly. It does, however, signal that Edelson / O+Z is actively prosecuting its appeal and has moved to the record-preparation phase. Cowan DeBaets' parallel absence from the district docket through August 31 leaves open whether that firm has filed its own designation directly on the Ninth Circuit docket (where it would not appear here) or has not yet done so; that distinction matters because a failure to timely designate transcripts can draw a Ninth Circuit clerk's default notice. Neither the district docket nor any available public source confirms the status of Cowan DeBaets' transcript designation. No party has moved for consolidation of the two appeals, and no consolidation order has appeared on the district court's docket.

The class's recovery posture is unchanged. Anthropic's payment obligations run independently of the fee appeals — no party has moved for a stay — and the $450 million first installment (Scheduled Payment 1) remains due September 25, 2026. The next concrete milestones are: (1) Anthropic's $450 million Scheduled Payment 1 on September 25; and (2) Ninth Circuit scheduling orders establishing opening-brief deadlines for Nos. 26-5391 and 26-5455, which the circuit clerk typically issues within the first weeks after a case opens and which will set the appellate briefing clock for both fee disputes.

The only docket entry with analytical weight in the current window is Dkt. 190 (filed August 28), a motion to approve a compromise under Rule 9019.
items.body_md:
On August 31, the Bankruptcy Notification Center docketed Dkt. 191, a certificate of notice tied to an order — filing infrastructure, not a substantive event. The only docket entry with analytical weight in the current window is Dkt. 190 (filed August 28), a motion to approve a compromise under Rule 9019. A Rule 9019 motion is substantive: it seeks court authorization for a settlement of some claim, dispute, or controversy affecting the estate, and if approved it will bind creditors to whatever terms the estate negotiated. The docket metadata does not identify the counterparty, the subject matter, or the dollar amount; the underlying pleading must be pulled directly from CM/ECF or __[Verita Global](https://veritaglobal.net/poolin)__ to assess materiality to recovery. Under the District of New Jersey's standard practice, a Rule 9019 motion carries a 21-day objection period running from the filing date, placing the objection deadline at approximately September 18 — the same date as the sale hearing before Judge O'Hagan. That overlap is operationally significant: any creditor or party in interest contesting the settlement terms must act on a compressed timeline coinciding with the most consequential hearing on the docket.

The qualified bid deadline arrives one week from today, September 8. Competing bids received by that date trigger the West Texas mining asset auction on September 10 at 10:00 a.m. Eastern at Archer & Greiner's offices in Voorhees, New Jersey (or virtually, or at another debtors-designated location). If no qualified bids clear the stalking-horse floor, the September 10 auction is a formality and Thor CALAP LLC acquires the Pyote and Tarbush sites on its existing $52 million terms. Sale objections are due September 16 at 5:00 p.m. Eastern; the sale hearing before Judge O'Hagan follows on September 18 at 11:00 a.m.

The next concrete milestone is September 8 — the qualified bid deadline — which will determine whether the auction is competitive or a single-bidder formality. The Rule 9019 compromise at Dkt. 190 warrants immediate attention from any creditor tracking recovery exposure; until the underlying motion is reviewed, its impact on estate value or claim treatment cannot be assessed.

items.lede: On August 30, a deposition notice was filed in Case No. 26-11217 as Dkt. 89, the sole entry since the August 28 discovery hearing. The docket caption — "Deposition - Notice" — does not disclose the noticed witness or the scheduled date.
items.body_md:
On August 30, a deposition notice was filed in Case No. 26-11217 as Dkt. 89, the sole entry since the August 28 discovery hearing. The docket caption — "Deposition - Notice" — does not disclose the noticed witness or the scheduled date. Given the posture coming out of the August 28 hearing on Skillz's motion to compel (Dkt. 73), two readings are available: Papaya has noticed a deposition consistent with its amended deposition notice strategy telegraphed by Dkt. 77, or Skillz has noticed a witness following a ruling at the August 28 hearing that granted some or all of the relief it sought. No order resolving Dkt. 73 appears on the docket as of this briefing, which itself carries information — if Judge Walrath granted the motion to compel from the bench, a written order would typically follow within a day or two, and its absence suggests either the matter was taken under advisement or the parties are working through a negotiated production protocol.

The August 28 hearing outcome remains unconfirmed on the docket. No written order on the motion to compel has appeared. The absence of a ruling order does not foreclose a bench decision, but until Dkt. 87 — filed August 28 and labeled only "Order" in the prior context — is confirmed to address Dkt. 73 specifically, its scope cannot be assumed. Dkt. 88, a notice of appearance filed the same day, and Dkt. 85, a minute entry, are procedural and carry no independent bearing on recovery or timing.

On the Israeli track, 
Judge Lushi-Abudi rejected Papaya's motion to convene creditors' meetings to vote on its proposed debt settlement, ruling that the plan — which relies solely on operating profits — must be strengthened
, per the __[Firy/FIRY press release carried by StockTitan](https://www.stocktitan.net/news/FIRY/israeli-court-says-papaya-gaming-should-improve-its-debt-settlement-81are4y0jeia.html)__ dated August 26. 
The court stated that Papaya should improve its proposed debt settlement by adding funding beyond just operating profits, and at the August 25 hearing the judge mentioned that the proposal could also be improved by increasing the amount paid into the arrangement following its approval.
 That dynamic reinforces Skillz's interest in maximizing the Delaware discovery record: the broader and more granular the picture of Papaya's financial position before Judge Walrath rules on recognition, the stronger Skillz's factual foundation for contesting the terms of any plan that surfaces in the Israeli proceeding. The next identifiable milestone is the appearance of a written order on Dkt. 73 or a further scheduling directive from Judge Walrath setting the recognition hearing date.

items.body_md:
On August 24, the SEC issued Release No. 106177 in an administrative proceeding (File No. 3-22435), extending the deadline to submit a Proposed Plan of Distribution — most likely to August 26, 2027 — after the Division received four public comments on a proposed plan it published for comment on June 29, 2026. 
The Commission published a Notice of Proposed Plan of Distribution on June 29, 2026 under Rule 1103, inviting public comment through July 29, 2026, and received four comments raising various issues before issuing this extension on August 24, 2026.
 The practical consequence for Class 5 claimants is significant: the August 20 deadline the SEC faced — under the Second Extension Order (Release No. 104875, February 20, 2026, File No. 3-22382) — has now been superseded, and the Commission's own published distribution methodology will not be finalized for another year. The relationship between File No. 3-22382 (the prior Tai Mo Shan extension orders) and File No. 3-22435 (Release No. 106177) requires confirmation against the full order text; the operative point for recovery posture is that the __[SEC's enforcement docket](https://www.sec.gov/files/litigation/admin/2026/34-106177.pdf)__ reflects a further extension well past August 20, meaning no distribution framework for the $123.1 million Fair Fund will issue in the near term.


The plan, once submitted, must define investor eligibility, loss calculations, claim requirements, and payment procedures; the deadline does not trigger payouts. Coordination with Terraform's separate bankruptcy recovery remains unresolved, and claims in the bankruptcy proceeding do not automatically establish eligibility for this fund.
 For Class 5 holders with overlapping losses in both tracks, this extension compounds timing uncertainty: the bankruptcy wind-down runs through December 31, 2026, but the parallel Fair Fund track — which could affect net recovery on duplicate losses — now trails it by a year or more. The SEC's apparent reason for the further extension is the public comment process: 
the Commission published a Notice of Proposed Plan under Rule 1103, with the comment period closing July 29, 2026, suggesting the four comments received required the Division to rework or respond to the proposed methodology before a final plan can be submitted.


Dkt. 1325, filed today, is a rescheduled hearing notice — procedural and routine, carrying no independent effect on recovery or claim allowance. The authorization motion filed August 19 (Dkt. 1321) remains unresolved on the public record, with no corresponding order yet appearing on the docket. The next fixed milestone is December 31, 2026 — the court-extended wind-down deadline — with the Jump Trading litigation and *Chang v. Terraform Labs Wind Down Trust* adversary proceeding the primary substantive resolution triggers ahead of that date. On the Fair Fund track, the operative question is now whether the SEC's next extension order (Release No. 106177) covers the same File No. 3-22382 proceeding as the prior Tai Mo Shan orders, or a distinct but related administrative matter; confirmation would come from the full order text available at the __[SEC enforcement docket](https://www.sec.gov/files/litigation/admin/2026/34-106177.pdf)__.

items.lede: On August 25, a party filed Dkt. 483 — an Opposition/Response to Motion — the only new docket entry since yesterday's briefing. The motion being opposed is not identified in the docket text as reproduced here.
items.body_md:
On August 25, a party filed Dkt. 483 — an Opposition/Response to Motion — the only new docket entry since yesterday's briefing. The motion being opposed is not identified in the docket text as reproduced here. Given the live motions practice in this case, the most plausible target is Google's August 21 Administrative Motion to Consider Whether Cases Should Be Related (Dkt. 478), whose response deadline was set at August 25 — the same date Dkt. 483 was filed. If that is the motion being opposed, the filing reflects a party — most likely the plaintiff class — resisting Google's effort to link this proceeding to one or more related cases. The case-relation motion, if granted, could shift judicial assignment or coordinate discovery and briefing schedules in ways that affect litigation pace and cost for both sides; if denied, each proceeding continues on its own track. Until Dkt. 483's full text is pulled from PACER, the identity of the filing party, the motion it targets, and the arguments advanced remain unverified and are not stated here.

The more consequential open question from yesterday remains unresolved in any available source: the outcome of the Dkt. 482 omnibus order — which adjudicates class certification, Google's sanctions motion, the outstanding intervention motion (Dkt. 468, Lee Child/Andrew Child/Girlcomix), and three motions for miscellaneous relief — has not been reported by any secondary outlet as of this briefing. The full text of Dkt. 482 on PACER is the controlling document. Until it is pulled, the class's shape, the sanctions disposition, and whether the intervenors were admitted remain unverified. The practical consequence is significant: class certification in this case defines the universe of copyright holders who can share in any statutory-damages recovery, and the per-work structure of § 504(c) means that the breadth of the certified class — authors only, publishers included, works defined by training vs. ingestion — directly sets the ceiling on Google's aggregate exposure.

The next concrete milestone is the resolution of the Dkt. 478 case-relation motion, which is now fully briefed with Dkt. 483's opposition and ripe for ruling. No hearing date is visible in the docket text for that motion. On the merits track, the full text of Dkt. 482 — available on PACER at 5:23-cv-03440 — remains the priority pull; it is the document that determines where this case goes from here.

items.body_md:
On August 12, at least two parties filed oppositions (Dkts. 51 and 52) and one filed an objection (Dkt. 56) against what the docket labels confirm are distinct contested matters, accompanied by a supporting declaration (Dkt. 53) and a stipulation (Dkt. 57) — the heaviest single day of adversarial activity in this case since the first-day hearing. The docket does not yet identify the targets of those filings by description in the materials available to this desk, but the case context narrows the candidates sharply. The CRO compensation notice (Dkt. 43, filed August 5) carried an opposition deadline of August 19 and sought court authorization for insider-adjacent compensation — the CRO, Leslie Gladstone, being named in Dkt. 43's attachments — making it a live target for the U.S. Trustee or judgment creditors. The Manatt employment application (Dkt. 42, filed August 5) is the other obvious target; contested retention applications, particularly where the estate is essentially a litigation-liability vehicle funded by a CEO-owned DIP lender, attract U.S. Trustee scrutiny on disinterestedness and connections. The employment application at Dkt. 49 (filed August 10) is too recent to have drawn a deadline-compliant response by August 12 under standard notice periods. Until the full text of Dkts. 51, 52, 53, 56, and 57 is reviewed on PACER, their precise targets remain unverified; the desk flags this and will confirm at next update. What is clear from the docket structure — two oppositions plus a supporting declaration filed the same day as a separate objection — is that at least two distinct contested matters were briefed simultaneously on August 12, a pattern inconsistent with ordinary course and consistent with coordinated creditor or U.S. Trustee opposition.

The Errors/Deficiencies notice at Dkt. 59 (BNC, August 13) and the Generic Order at Dkt. 60 (August 13) are almost certainly related: the deficiency notice identifies a filing that failed to meet local-rule requirements, and the generic order likely resolves or memorializes the correction. This is procedural and carries no independent weight on recovery, though a deficiency on a retention or compensation filing could slow the authorization clock. Dkts. 54 and 55 are certificates of service, and Dkt. 58 is a proof of service (CSD 3010); all three are filing infrastructure and are omitted. The stipulation at Dkt. 57 is substantive in classification — stipulations in contested Chapter 11 matters affect legal rights — but its substance is unverified; if it reflects an agreed resolution of one of the contested matters briefed the same day, it is material to recovery posture, and the desk will confirm.

The contested posture on these professional-retention and compensation matters matters for creditors beyond the immediate cost. 
The two principal judgments — approximately $245 million in the De la Torre class action and approximately $157 million in the CFPB tribal-lending action — together with roughly $45 million in additional pending litigation and about $5 million in trade debt and professional fees, constitute substantially all of the debtor's prepetition obligations
, against reported assets of $1 million to $10 million. In that context, professional fees and CRO compensation drawn from the estate — funded by a ~$4 million DIP facility 
owned by the debtor's CEO
 — are not administrative minutiae; they directly compress whatever is available to unsecured creditors. Vigorous opposition to these applications signals that at least one party is treating the fee burn as a recovery issue, not a routine creditor courtesy. The next concrete milestone is the August 19 opposition deadline on the CRO compensation notice (Dkt. 43), which will either close the briefing on that motion or extend it if further responses arrive — and, depending on the scope of Dkt. 56's objection, the court may consolidate argument on the professional matters at a single hearing.
